title: The Story of the Telephone
summary: How the telephone grew from the telegraph and Alexander Graham Bell's 1876 invention into the mobile phones people carry today.
poll: The telephone is the most important invention of the last two hundred years.

versions.title: The First Phone
versions.text:
Do you talk on a phone? Long ago, there were no phones. To send a message, you wrote a note. It could take weeks to get there.

Then came a new way to send words. Clicks went down a long wire. Each set of clicks stood for a letter. But you could not hear a voice.

A man named Bell had a big plan. He wanted to send a voice down a wire. In the year 1876, he did it! He had found a way to invent the phone.

His first words on the phone went to his helper. He said, "Mr. Watson, come here. I want to see you." Mr. Watson was in the next room. He heard the words!

How does a phone work? Your voice makes a sound. The phone turns the sound into a signal. The signal zips down a wire. Then a phone at the far end turns it back to sound.

Phones got small. In 1973, a man made the first call on a phone he could hold. It was big and heavy. Now we hold small phones. We send a message or a photo in a flash.

Do you ever call your grandparents on the phone? Not very long ago, telephones did not exist at all, so anyone who wanted to communicate with someone far away had to write a letter, which could take weeks to arrive.

In 1876, after many experiments, he received a patent, an official document stating that an invention belongs to its creator. Then the receiver at the other end converts the signal back into sound, so the listener hears your words almost instantly.

versions.title: The Story of the Telephone
versions.text:
Do you ever call your grandparents on the phone? Not very long ago, telephones did not exist at all, and anyone who wanted to communicate with a distant friend had to write a letter that might take weeks to arrive.

During the 1800s, a faster invention appeared. The telegraph could transmit messages along wires as short and long electrical pulses, with each pattern representing a letter. Although it was remarkably quick, it could not carry the sound of a human voice.

Alexander Graham Bell, a teacher who worked with deaf students, dreamed of sending speech along a wire, partly because his own mother had lost most of her hearing. In 1876, after many experiments, he received a patent, an official document stating that an invention belongs to its creator. However, another inventor, Elisha Gray, had submitted papers describing a similar idea on the same day that Bell sent in his own. A few days later, Bell spoke the first clear words over his telephone when he called to his assistant in the neighboring room: "Mr. Watson, come here; I want to see you."

How does a telephone actually work? When you speak, your voice makes the air vibrate, and a microphone inside the phone converts these vibrations into an electrical signal that travels to another phone, where a speaker converts the signal back into sound.

Early telephones could not dial one another directly. Instead, an operator seated at a large switchboard connected each call manually, plugging cables into the correct sockets, until automatic equipment eventually took over this responsibility.

In 1973, an engineer made the first call on a handheld mobile phone, although the device was bulky and weighed about a kilogram. Mobile phones are wireless, because they send signals through the air to nearby towers rather than along a wire. Many calls now travel as flashes of light through thin glass cables laid across the ocean floor. Today, smartphones allow us to send a message, a photograph, or a video across the world within seconds. In less than one hundred fifty years, the telephone has helped revolutionize the way people communicate.

versions.title: The Telephone: From Wires to Wireless
versions.text:
Do you perhaps telephone your grandparents with any regularity? Not especially long ago, in historical terms, telephones did not exist whatsoever, and anyone wishing to communicate with a distant relative had no recourse but to compose a letter that might require several weeks merely to arrive at its destination.

During the nineteenth century, a considerably faster means of long-distance communication emerged. The telegraph proved capable of transmitting messages along wires as patterns of short and long electrical pulses, with each distinct pattern representing a particular letter of the alphabet, yet although remarkably efficient for its era, it remained entirely incapable of carrying the actual sound of a human voice.

Alexander Graham Bell, a teacher who worked closely with deaf students, dreamed persistently of transmitting speech itself along a wire, motivated in part by the fact that his own mother had lost the majority of her hearing. In 1876, following numerous painstaking experiments, he received a patent, an official document certifying that a particular invention belongs exclusively to its creator, although another inventor, Elisha Gray, had coincidentally submitted papers describing a remarkably similar concept on the very same day that Bell submitted his own application. A few days thereafter, Bell spoke the first genuinely intelligible words ever transmitted over his telephone when he summoned his assistant from an adjoining room: "Mr. Watson, come here; I want to see you."

How, precisely, does a telephone actually accomplish this feat? When an individual speaks, the resulting vocal vibrations disturb the surrounding air, and a microphone embedded within the device converts these physical vibrations into a corresponding electrical signal that travels along a wire to a second, distant telephone, where an internal speaker converts the signal back into audible, recognizable sound.

Early telephones could not dial one another directly without assistance, so a human operator seated at an enormous switchboard connected each individual call manually, physically inserting cables into the appropriate sockets, until automatic switching equipment eventually assumed this repetitive responsibility entirely, a development that allowed the total number of telephone subscribers to multiply rapidly throughout the twentieth century as networks steadily expanded across cities, entire countries, and ultimately whole continents.

In 1973, an engineer placed the first call ever made on a handheld mobile telephone, although the device itself was remarkably cumbersome and weighed approximately a full kilogram. Mobile phones are properly described as wireless, since they transmit signals through the surrounding atmosphere to nearby communication towers rather than along any physical wire, and numerous international calls today travel instead as pulses of light through microscopically thin glass fibers contained within cables stretched across the entire ocean floor. Today, smartphones enable us to share a written message, a photograph, or a video recording across the entire world within mere seconds, and in less than one hundred fifty years, the telephone has unquestionably helped revolutionize the fundamental way humanity communicates with itself.

versions.title: The Telephone: From Wires to Wireless
versions.text:
Do you perhaps telephone your grandparents with any meaningful regularity? Not especially long ago, in strictly historical terms, telephones did not exist in any form whatsoever, and anyone wishing to communicate with a geographically distant relative had no recourse but to compose a handwritten letter that might require several weeks merely to arrive at its intended destination.

During the course of the nineteenth century, a considerably faster means of long-distance communication gradually emerged. The telegraph proved capable of transmitting coded messages along wires as patterns of short and long electrical pulses, with each distinct pattern corresponding to a particular letter of the alphabet, yet although remarkably efficient for an invention of its era, it remained entirely incapable of carrying the actual acoustic sound of a human voice across any distance.

Alexander Graham Bell, a teacher who worked closely and extensively with deaf students, dreamed persistently of transmitting speech itself along a wire, motivated in considerable part by the fact that his own mother had lost the overwhelming majority of her hearing earlier in life. In 1876, following numerous painstaking and iterative experiments, he successfully received a patent, an official legal document formally certifying that a particular invention belongs exclusively to its creator, although another inventor, Elisha Gray, had coincidentally submitted paperwork describing a remarkably similar underlying concept on the very same day that Bell submitted his own competing application. A mere few days thereafter, Bell spoke the first genuinely intelligible words ever transmitted over his nascent telephone when he summoned his assistant from an adjoining room with the now-famous instruction: "Mr. Watson, come here; I want to see you."

How, precisely, does a telephone mechanism actually accomplish this remarkable feat of communication? When an individual speaks, the resulting vocal vibrations disturb and compress the surrounding air molecules, and a microphone embedded within the device converts these physical acoustic vibrations into a corresponding electrical signal that travels instantaneously along a wire to a second, geographically distant telephone, where an internal speaker converts the transmitted signal back into audible, perfectly recognizable sound.

Early telephones could not dial one another directly without human assistance, and so a trained operator seated at an enormous switchboard connected each individual call manually, physically inserting cables into the appropriate electrical sockets, until automatic switching equipment eventually assumed this repetitive responsibility entirely, a technological development that subsequently allowed the total number of telephone subscribers to multiply with extraordinary rapidity throughout the twentieth century as networks steadily expanded across individual cities, entire countries, and ultimately whole continents simultaneously.

In 1973, an engineer placed the first telephone call ever made on a genuinely handheld mobile device, although the device itself was remarkably cumbersome in practice and weighed approximately a full kilogram in total. Mobile telephones are properly and technically described as wireless, since they transmit signals through the surrounding atmosphere to nearby communication towers rather than along any physical conducting wire, and numerous international telephone calls today instead travel as discrete pulses of light through microscopically thin glass fibers contained within specialized cables stretched across the entirety of the ocean floor. Today, ubiquitous smartphones enable us to share a written message, a photograph, or an entire video recording across the breadth of the world within mere seconds, and in considerably less than one hundred fifty years, the telephone has unquestionably helped revolutionize the fundamental manner in which humanity communicates with itself across every conceivable distance.

checklist: I explained the steps in order.
I used vibrate and receiver correctly.
I used details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: When you speak into a telephone, your voice makes the air vibrate. The phone changes these vibrations into an electric signal that travels along a wire to your friend's phone. Then the receiver on the other end changes the signal back into sound, so your friend can hear your voice.

HIGH.prompt: Choose one change in telephone history (the switchboard, automatic equipment, or wireless phones) and explain how it changed the way people communicate.
checklist: I chose one change and described it accurately.
I explained its effect on communication.
I used evidence and key words from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I chose the change from switchboard operators to automatic equipment. In early telephones, an operator had to connect every call by hand, which made communication slow and dependent on another person. Once automatic machines took over this job, calls could be transmitted directly between people without waiting for an operator, which made communication faster and more private. This change helped revolutionize how quickly people could reach one another, setting the stage for the instant electrical communication we rely on today.
